title: Building for the web, one page at a time
description: A few thoughts on keeping web projects clear, useful, and enjoyable to work on.
paragraphs: The best websites do not need to be complicated. They need to help people find what they came for, understand what they are looking at, and move naturally to the next thing.
A good starting point is a clear structure. Give every page a purpose, keep navigation predictable, and make the content the most important part of the experience.
Next.js helps organise that work with file-based routing, reusable components, and flexible rendering strategies. Start with the fundamentals, then add complexity only when the project needs it.
This project follows the same idea. The home, blog, news, and product pages each have one job, and the shared header and footer keep the experience consistent as you move between them.

title: Why the small details matter
description: Readable type, useful spacing, and consistent navigation make a project easier to use.
paragraphs: People notice when an interface makes their next step obvious. They also notice when labels are unclear, links move around, or a page feels crowded.
Small decisions add up: a comfortable reading width, consistent heading levels, visible focus states, and navigation that works on a phone.
These details are not decoration. They reduce friction and let the content speak for itself.
A quick check at 375, 768, and 1280 pixels catches most layout problems before they reach a reader. If the page still works at those widths, it usually works everywhere in between.

title: Learning by building small projects
description: A focused project is often the fastest way to understand a new framework.
paragraphs: When learning a framework, it is tempting to start with a large product idea. A smaller project can teach the same core concepts with fewer distractions.
A blog is a useful example because it naturally includes a home page, a collection of posts, individual detail pages, and shared navigation.
Build one route at a time. Test it, understand how data reaches the page, and document the rendering choices you make.
Over time those small choices become a reference you can reuse: a pattern for static pages, one for request-time data, and one for content that should refresh on a schedule.
